evidence: src/application/dtos.ts defines toOrderDto and toStockLevelDto once; the cancel, get, list-by-state, place and transition use cases all import toOrderDto, and list-stock-levels imports toStockLevelDto.

Every use case gets its persistence through injected domain ports: OrderRepository (cancel, get, list-by-state, place, transition) or ProductRepository (list-stock-levels). No file uses a database or ORM directly.
place-order-use-case.ts: assertExecuteRule is the only customerId validation in the unit.
Order state changes go through domain methods (order.cancel() in cancel-order-use-case.ts, order.moveTo(target) in transition-order-use-case.ts), so the use cases do not repeat them.

cancel-order-use-case.ts, get-order-use-case.ts and transition-order-use-case.ts repeat the same `if (!order) throw new NotFoundError(...)` guard. I judged it boilerplate error handling, not a duplicated domain rule.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: All seven files serve one concern: application use cases for orders and stock levels, plus their DTO mapping. Persistence is reached only through the domain ports OrderRepository and ProductRepository. No file builds a database or ORM client. DTO mapping is defined once, in dtos.ts (toOrderDto and toStockLevelDto), and every use case calls it rather than repeating the mapping inline. The customerId-required check exists only in place-order-use-case.ts (assertExecuteRule). Order state rules stay in the domain behind order.cancel() and order.moveTo(), and stock reservation stays behind StockReservationService. The not-found guard in the cancel, get and transition use cases is the same one-line error-handling idiom repeated, not a copied business rule or invariant, so I did not treat it as a violation. A stricter reading of the duplication clause could count it. No candidate flags were raised.
